assessments.reasoning: Printed pp. 63–65 and the summary on pp. 88–89 distinguish receiver identity from lookup origin. The Four instance receives result3 and keeps that identity when the method in Three uses super. The search for test then starts at Two, the superclass of Three, and yields 2.

challenge.method: Trace example4 result3 using the hierarchy and compare the hypothetical Three override on printed p. 65. Check the use of super as an argument on p. 64.
challenge.results: First matching result3 is in Three. The direct super send starts at Two and yields 2 even if Three hypothetically provides test returning 3. A receiver-superclass interpretation would start at Three and wrongly choose 3 in that case. A use of super purely as an argument leaves the receiver object unchanged and does not set the lookup origin of a send.

limitations: The result covers super in the receiver position of a send within a documented instance method. Ordinary self and super used as an argument have distinct lookup consequences.
Direct documentary review of the 1983 edition. No Smalltalk runtime was used.
